definition: Correlation describes how closely two things are related — when two assets are highly correlated, their prices tend to move together, though this does not necessarily mean one causes the other.
core_idea: Correlation can arise either from a genuine shared cause or from random chance, so a statistical relationship between two series is not by itself evidence of a causal link.
key_points: High correlation means two assets' prices tend to move together.
Correlation may or may not reflect a causal relationship.
Correlation can be produced by random chance rather than a real shared driver.
Correlation is a key input to many option pricing models used in energy markets.
relationships: Feeds into option pricing models in energy markets.
trading_implications: Expressing relationships precisely (e.g., '40 percent correlated') removes ambiguity compared to vague statements like 'they act alike most of the time.'
caveats: Assuming correlation implies causation: the author cites the NFL Super Bowl 'indicator' (stock market historically rising more often when an NFC team wins) as a correlation with no plausible causal link, and warns that over-precise use of coincidental correlations is misleading.
